summary:
Same-sex relations are illegal in Eswatini for men and women throughout the country as of 12 March 2026. Legal gender recognition is not available, so a trans visitor's passport and other identity documents are read exactly as issued, with no administrative route to align them with lived gender.

Eswatini recognises no same-sex relationships, and a trans visitor travelling in what would be locally classed as a same-sex relationship falls under the criminal law. In June 2012 Prime Minister Barnabas Sibusiso Dlamini said that people of the same sex could not even go to regional offices to get married and that the country was not ready to consider the question; in 2014 press secretary Percy Simelane said the government was monitoring the situation with a view to taking a legal position.

No broad legal protections against discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity exist in Eswatini in areas such as education, health, housing and employment. Whatever protection exists sits in policy documents rather than in enforceable law.

Organisational recognition is administratively blocked. The registrar of companies refused to register an LGBTI group in July 2019, and officials refused to register Eswatini Sexual and Gender Minorities in June 2019 on grounds of morality. In April 2022 the High Court upheld that refusal while accepting that the constitution protects LGBTQ persons' rights to freedom of association, privacy and expression. LGBTI organisations cannot register.

Access to care carries documented discrimination. A 2019 survey found that 59% of LGBTQ respondents had been discriminated against or treated disrespectfully at public health facilities and 30% had been denied healthcare services; the survey measured LGBTQ people generally rather than trans people specifically, and its fieldwork closed in 2019.

Targeted violence is documented with dates. In March 2015 a 26-year-old lesbian woman from Nhlangano was murdered by a man who did not want to be in the presence of lesbians, and a few months earlier a gay man was murdered in the same town. The most recent documented case in this record is from March 2015; no later instance is documented.

Official hostility is on the record. A 2021 US State Department report noted that some traditional, religious and government officials criticised same-sex sexual conduct as neither morally Swati nor Christian. In 2012 former Foreign Affairs Minister Mgwagwa Gamedze rejected a UN working group call for an LGBTQ protection law on the grounds that so few gay people lived in Eswatini that drafting one was not worth the effort, and in May 2017 the UN Human Rights Committee pressed the government on measures to protect people from discrimination and violence based on sexual orientation and gender identity.

Counterweight policy exists on paper. The National Guidelines for Adolescent Sexual and Reproductive Health (2021) state that the right to equality includes freedom from discrimination because of sex or sexual orientation, define gender-based violence to include violence directed at a person based on gender identity or perceived adherence to norms of masculinity and femininity, and name LGBT people as a key population at higher risk of gender-based violence. The National Strategy to End Violence 2023-2027 lists sexual orientation or identity among its inclusivity principles, and the 2017 Broadcasting Guidelines Services and 2022 Broadcasting (Content) Guidelines bar licensees from broadcasting material that sanctions, glamorises or incites violence or hatred on grounds including sexual orientation.
tangentialFactors:
Freedom House's Freedom in the World 2024 rates Eswatini Not Free with an overall score of 17/100, comprising Political Rights 1/40 and Civil Liberties 16/60, describing an absolute monarchy with severely restricted civic space. The BTI 2024 country report places the refusal to register LGBTQ+ groups inside a wider pattern of restricted political formations, meetings and recruitment, in an environment where 'Mswati must fall' had become a common protest slogan.

Public LGBT visibility has nonetheless been documented. The first Eswatini Pride was declared a great success in July 2018, and in June 2021 LGBTQI+ persons conducted a virtual Pride celebration without incident. In December 2018 a church in Swaziland welcoming LGBTIQ people reopened, reported alongside no let-up on discrimination in the kingdom.
localsOnly:
Rock of Hope states that with no legislation recognising LGBTIs or protecting gender identity, LGBTQ people cannot be open about their orientation or gender identity for fear of rejection and discrimination, and most choose to remain in the closet or move to South Africa.

Same-sex couples are prohibited from adopting children, while prospective heterosexual adoptive parents may be single, married or divorced.

Health policy contains specific commitments. Section 4.3 of the 2013 National Policy on Sexual and Reproductive Health requires the Ministry of Health to make family planning information and services available regardless of sex, gender, age, status, sexual orientation and religion. In February 2012 public health officials ran a Valentine's Day campaign urging gay people to test for HIV, and Deputy Director of Health Simon Zwane said the Health Ministry was extending HIV counselling and testing to same-sex couples, a move LGBTQ groups welcomed. The 2021 National Social Security Policy defines equity as free from discrimination including sexual orientation.

A 2013 survey found that 43% of lesbian and transgender respondents had attempted suicide in the past year and 78% regularly used intoxicating substances to feel normal. The fieldwork closed in 2013 and the figures describe residents, not visitors.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not state the statute or penalty under which same-sex relations are criminalised, and records no arrest or prosecution of an individual under that law. Enforcement frequency is not sourced.

No entry, visa or border-screening rules specific to trans travellers are sourced for Eswatini, and document-marker treatment at the border is not documented here.

No trans-specific violence rate or count is sourced. The record contains no documented killing of a trans person; the two documented killings are of a lesbian woman and a gay man, both from 2015.

Whether the April 2022 High Court ruling on registration has been appealed or implemented is not sourced.

The 2019 healthcare survey measured LGBTQ respondents and the 2013 survey measured lesbian and transgender respondents; neither measured trans visitors, and both windows closed years ago.

Bathroom and facilities rules, and any hate-crime sentencing enhancement covering gender identity, are not sourced for this jurisdiction.
